title: When you don't feel well
goal: Say which body part hurts, name common complaints, buy medicine at a pharmacy, and ask for help in an emergency.
bekal: using the pattern *masakit ang* + body part + possessor
naming complaints with *may* and with forms like *nilalagnat*
asking for help clearly and quickly

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Sa botika
dialogs.intro: Budi wakes up feeling unwell after getting caught in the rain yesterday. Mia takes him to the pharmacy at the end of the street.

lines.speaker: Mia:
lines.text: Kuya, ang pula ng mata mo. Ayos ka lang ba?
lines.id: Bro, your eyes are so red. Are you okay?
lines.literal: big-bro, how red of eye your. fine you just Q?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Hindi masyado. Masakit ang ulo ko at may sipon ako.
lines.id: Not really. My head hurts and I have a runny nose.
lines.literal: not very. painful the head my and there's cold I.

lines.id: A little. I got rained on yesterday, you see.

lines.id: Come on, let's go to the pharmacy.

notes: **Masakit ang ulo ko** is literally "painful the head my" — the adjective first, the thing after, exactly the pattern from unit 3. English says "my head hurts"; Tagalog flips the order, and this pattern works for every complaint.

**Nilalagnat ka ba?** uses an interesting form: illness is treated as something that **befalls** a person, not a state they possess. Its cousins: *sinisipon ako* (I've caught a cold), *inuubo ako* (I'm coughing), *sinusuka ako* (I'm throwing up).
**May sipon ako** is the simpler form and just as correct. For beginners, the pattern *may* + complaint + pronoun covers nearly every need: *may lagnat ako*, *may ubo ako*, *may sugat ako*.

**Naulanan ako** means "I got caught in the rain" — the prefix *na-* with the suffix *-an* marks something that happens to the doer against their will. Its cousins: *nabasa* (got wet), *nasunog* (got burned), *nahulog* (fell).
**A botika is a pharmacy**, and in the Philippines pharmacies may sell many medicines without a prescription. Those that need one are called *reseta*, and the pharmacist will ask for it if needed.

**Magpatingin sa doktor** is literally "have yourself looked at by a doctor". The prefix *magpa-* means having someone else do something for you — a form you'll learn fully at A2, but this phrase is worth memorizing whole now.
**Kung means "if"** and always stands in front of the condition: *Kung masakit pa bukas, pumunta ka sa doktor.* For a hypothetical "if" that didn't happen, use *kung sana*.
**Walang laman ang tiyan** = "the stomach has no content", Tagalog for an empty stomach. Note *wala* again as the negator of existence, as in unit 6.
**Ayos ka lang ba?** is the most common question when someone looks unwell or has just fallen. The standard answers are *Ayos lang* or *Okay lang* — both are equally common.

grammars.title: Saying which body part hurts
body: There are three patterns, all equally correct. Pick whichever comes most easily.
after: *Pakiramdam* means "bodily feeling" and is used for complaints with no clear location. The question: *Kumusta ang pakiramdam mo?* — "how are you feeling?"
To ask where it hurts: *Saan masakit?* or *Ano ang masakit?* A doctor will ask exactly that.
To say you're getting better: *Mas mabuti na ako* or *Gumaling na ako.*

grammars.title: Body parts
body: A few have Malay/Indonesian cousins (*mata* eye, *balat* skin, *buto* bone), but most you'll simply need to learn.
after: *Kamay* means hand, and it's where *kamayan* — eating with your hands, from unit 17 — comes from.
*Paa* means the foot from the ankle down; for the whole leg use *binti* (lower leg) or *hita* (thigh).
Body parts nearly always come with a possessor: *ulo **ko***, *kamay **mo***, *mata **niya***. Without it, the sentence sounds left hanging.

blocks.text: **Dengue fever** is an illness whose name you should know, because it's a real risk in the Philippines. If a fever comes with red spots or severe joint pain, don't wait: *Kailangan ko pong magpatingin sa doktor ngayon.*

blocks.title: At a clinic or hospital
items: *Gusto ko pong magpatingin sa doktor.* — I'd like to see a doctor.
*May appointment po ba kailangan?* — Do I need an appointment?
*Magkano po ang konsulta?* — How much is the consultation?
*May allergy po ako sa …* — I'm allergic to …
*Buntis po ako.* — I'm pregnant.

blocks.text: The Philippines' national emergency number is **911**, the same as in the United States. Operators speak English, so in a panic you may use English entirely — that's not a failure of language, it's safety.

blocks.title: Sentences you hope you'll never need
items: *Hindi ako makahinga.* — I can't breathe.
*Nahimatay siya.* — He/she fainted.
*May dugo.* — There's blood.
*Dalhin po ninyo ako sa ospital.* — Please take me to the hospital.
My head hurts.
I have a fever.
I have a cold and a cough.
Do you have medicine for a stomachache?
Where's the nearest hospital?
Help!

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks with the right body part.
items: Masakit ang ____ ko, kailangan ko ng dentista. (tooth)
Masakit ang ____ ko, hindi ako makakain. (stomach)
Ang pula ng ____ mo. (eyes)
May sugat sa ____ ko. (hand)
Masakit ang ____ ko kakaupo buong araw. (back)

exercises.prompt: Choose the right sentence for each situation.
items: You want to buy fever medicine at a pharmacy. You say ____.
You want to see a doctor. You say ____.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
items: ko / ang / masakit / ulo
ako / lagnat / may
sipon / po / ba / para / gamot / sa / may / ?
sa / doktor / po / magpatingin / kayo
po / ako / nawawala

answers: Masakit ang ulo ko. — May lagnat ako. — May sipon at ubo ako. — May gamot po ba para sa sakit ng tiyan? — Nasaan ang pinakamalapit na ospital? — Tulong po!
May gamot po ba para sa lagnat? — Gusto ko pong magpatingin sa doktor. — May allergy po ako sa hipon. — Ayos ka lang ba? — Nawala po ang pasaporte ko.
